covers.quote: Adapt writing style with tone and voice
Adjust your style to meet user needs.
The appropriate level of formality depends on what the relationship is between content and its user.
The right voice for content will depend on the persona fit for the content.

rules.quote: Adapt tone and voice to engage users, so the content can meet their needs.
rules.specification: Suitability requires information about the intended users, purpose and context. The page does not prescribe one tone or voice for every document.
rules.violation_condition: The content’s tone or persona is inappropriate for its intended users, purpose or context.
when: Assess suitability for the particular audience and content type.
Ministerial briefs need not use the same tone and voice as speeches or website information.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the repeated audience-and-context instruction; G-2 keeps the different content contexts together.

rules.quote: Using the first person singular (the pronoun ‘I’) is rarely suitable in government content, except in correspondence.
rules.specification: ‘Rarely suitable’ makes this a review flag rather than an absolute prohibition. The page does not identify the exceptional suitable uses outside correspondence.
rules.violation_condition: The author uses the first-person singular pronoun ‘I’ in government content other than correspondence.
when: Applies to government content.
Correspondence is an explicit exception.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the correspondence exception and the qualified restriction in one check.

covers.quote: can use contractions and personal pronouns

rules.violation_condition: A contraction appears in content using formal tone.
when: Applies when the content uses formal tone.
Contractions are permitted in standard tone.
rules.why: G-2 limits the restriction to formal tone; G-3 records the standard-tone permission rather than making it another rule.

covers.quote: is literal – words are used with their dictionary meaning
doesn’t use metaphor, slang or idioms
Informal tone can use metaphors and idioms, which can have a negative effect on inclusion.

rules.quote: doesn’t use metaphors, idioms or slang.
rules.violation_condition: Formal-tone content uses words non-literally, or standard-tone content contains a metaphor or idiom.
when: Formal tone uses words literally, with their dictionary meanings.
Both formal and standard tone exclude metaphors and idioms.
Informal tone may use metaphors and idioms, although the page warns about their effects on inclusion and plain language.
rules.why: G-2 combines the tone-dependent figurative-language restrictions; G-3 records the informal-tone permission. Slang has a separate all-tone check.

covers.quote: doesn’t use metaphor, slang or idioms
doesn’t use metaphors, idioms or slang.

rules.quote: You should not use slang when writing on behalf of government.
rules.violation_condition: Slang appears in writing on behalf of government.
when: Applies when writing on behalf of government, regardless of tone.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 consolidate the slang restrictions into one check rather than flagging slang again for each tone.

rules.specification: This page names inclusive language as a property but does not supply the detailed criteria needed to operationalise it.
rules.violation_condition: Exclusionary or discriminatory language appears in content intended to use the recommended respectful government voice.
when: Applies to the respectful writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: G-1 keeps the specific inclusive-language property rather than adding a broad respectful-style rule.

rules.specification: Assess familiarity for the intended users. The page supplies no fixed vocabulary list or rare-word threshold.
rules.violation_condition: Ideas are expressed in vocabulary that is unnecessarily unfamiliar to the intended users rather than everyday words.
when: Applies to the respectful writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: G-1 selects the specific vocabulary property instead of creating an additional broad plain-language finding.

rules.quote: doesn’t use inflammatory language, such as name-calling or sarcasm
rules.violation_condition: Inflammatory wording, including name-calling or sarcasm, appears in content intended to use a respectful government voice.
when: Applies to the respectful writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: G-1 retains the specific inflammatory-language restriction; name-calling and sarcasm are instances of that check.

rules.specification: Assess how the wording treats readers; explaining a basic concept is not by itself evidence of condescension.
rules.violation_condition: The wording patronises readers or treats them as inferior.
when: Applies to the respectful writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: The one-finding test separates condescension from the distinct problem of excessive familiarity.

rules.specification: The page gives no boundary for ‘too familiar’; assessment requires the intended relationship with readers.
rules.violation_condition: The wording assumes an excessively familiar relationship with readers.
when: Applies to the respectful writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: The one-finding test separates excessive familiarity from speaking down to readers.

rules.violation_condition: Passive voice appears where the content is intended to use the recommended clear and direct writing style.
when: Applies to the clear and direct writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: G-1 keeps the specific grammatical-voice property rather than adding a duplicate clear-and-direct umbrella check.

rules.specification: Interpret concision as avoiding unnecessary wording or repetition, not as a numerical sentence-length or word-count limit.
rules.violation_condition: Avoidably wordy or repetitive content adds length without contributing to the message.
when: Applies to the clear and direct writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: G-1 retains concision as a specific property; E-4 avoids inventing a length threshold.

rules.specification: The page gives no organisational pattern or concrete structural test. Operational criteria would need to be supplied.
rules.violation_condition: The content lacks a coherent organisation of its ideas.
when: Applies to the clear and direct writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: G-1 retains organisation as a distinct property rather than folding it into vocabulary, grammar or concision.

covers.quote: relies on facts
Viewpoint affects perception of whether information is neutral or impartial.
Adjectives and adverbs can also affect whether the information comes across as fact or opinion.

rules.specification: Judge whether wording expresses or implies subjective evaluation. Personal pronouns, adjectives and adverbs are contextual cues, not automatically prohibited forms.
rules.violation_condition: Opinion or subjective framing appears in content intended to be objective and impartial.
when: Applies to the objective and impartial writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
Consider viewpoint and the effects of adjectives and adverbs.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the fact-versus-opinion wording; G-2 keeps viewpoint and word-choice cues within the same contextual check.

rules.specification: Assess partiality in context. The page provides no quantitative measure of balance.
rules.violation_condition: The content presents information in a one-sided or biased way despite its intended objective and impartial voice.
when: Applies to the objective and impartial writing style described as part of the suggested basic government voice.
rules.why: The one-finding test distinguishes biased selection or presentation from the separate presence of opinion.
